hints: Think separately about what controls the speed of the reaction and what controls how much gas you get in total.
Lower temperature slows the reaction down, so the second change must speed it back up to finish in the same time, while zinc is the limiting reagent in excess acid.
Look for the change that increases rate by lowering activation energy but is not used up, so the total moles of hydrogen stay exactly the same.
walkthrough:
**Write the reaction and spot the limiting reagent**

Think of it simply: zinc is used up to make the hydrogen gas, while the acid is in excess.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{Zn(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4\text{(aq) + H}_2\text{(g)}$$

**See what lower temperature does**

Lower temperature means particles have less kinetic energy and fewer successful collisions per second.
So the rate decreases and the reaction would normally take longer to finish.

**Apply the two conditions for experiment 2**

Same total volume of $\text{H}_2$ means the same moles of limiting reagent, so the mass of $\text{Zn}$ must be unchanged.
Same completion time despite lower temperature means something else must increase the rate by exactly the right amount without being used up.

**Conclude the compensating change**

A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, so it speeds up the reaction at the lower temperature.
It is not consumed, so the total amount of $\text{H}_2$ from the fixed mass of zinc stays the same.

options.A: A catalyst increases the rate without changing the total yield. It compensates for the slowing effect of lower temperature, so the same volume of hydrogen is produced in the same time.
options.B: Zinc is the limiting reagent because the acid is in excess. Adding more zinc would produce more moles of $\text{H}_2$ and increase the total gas volume, which contradicts the question.
options.C: The acid is already in excess, so adding a greater volume of the same dilute acid does not change the moles of zinc or significantly change the rate. It cannot make up for the slower rate at lower temperature.
options.D: Larger lumps have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, so the rate would decrease even further. Combined with lower temperature, the reaction would take much longer, not the same time.
